title: The white angel
sentences: White angel, white angel!…
Dream-vision of a starry night…
A faint, trembling mist-phantom on a moonlit distant hill…
As though it sits there motionless…
Its soul is a lone star shining through it.
Clear is the night sky; neither cloud nor bird crosses it.
The moon, half spent, watches the dear, lovely mist-shape with a lulling gaze,
and slowly, unremarked, sinks behind the greenish hill rising on the opposite horizon.
To the left, the gloomy ruins of an ancient castle lie on a volcano-shaped peak in the wooded wasteland,
half shadow, half skeleton of a fallen giant staring skyward in unthinking, deathly stillness.
To the right, a wearying plain.
Leaf-strewn land, hill here, stream there, tree and bush scattered about and the occasional white farmhouse.
All sleeps.
All is silent…
White angel, white angel!…
Only you wake sleepless.
One star after another goes down to rest.
The whole sky turns, only you sit there,
the white shadow cast upon the sky by an invisible soul above the pale-green distant hills; your star-soul shines brightly through your white mist-robe.
You flicker – you flicker.
Like the mirage's daughter forgotten there through the night.
When you appear, nature holds festival.
Not a leaf stirs on the trees.
On the sea the ships stand still.
But the first breeze dissolves your form, and your star goes far to shine in the boundless sky.
White angel, white angel!…
You were once a red rose.
A splendid red earthly angel.
Blessed was he who looked at you, blessed he whom you looked upon, and pardoning power was vested in your lips.
How fair, how alluring you remain even after your death; what you must have been in life!…
Even now you are a blessing to the people.
On quiet spring nights you sometimes appear.
Soft bell-tones ring out then across the countryside.
The people go to praise their God, who sent you forth.
There will be harvest, there will be grape-gathering, cellars and vaults will fill; praised be the Lord of heaven, the white angel has appeared…
What sorrow brings you to earth each spring, when the white rose and lily begin to bloom?
Cannot they open without you?
or perhaps you come to visit someone who cannot rise from the grave to meet you?…
Last July the Hungarian leader was marching toward Miskolc.
In a village not far off he halted for the night with his army.
He took lodging in the manor house, where of the noble family only the companion lady was present to receive him.
The revolutionary leader seldom caused inconvenience wherever he lodged; the cultivated lady, for her part, gladly fulfilled his every wish.
The leader's wound had gone three days without being rebound; they lifted him half-conscious from his carriage, and when they laid him down,
a fierce wound-fever broke out upon him, which until then the unceasing struggles of constant battles had not allowed to take hold.
The lady wished to help the doctors with the dressing of the wound.
She was horrified when she saw the dreadful deep gash that ran long across his handsome head, all the way to his brow.
– My God, what a terrible wound!
– Would that it were mortal, if only the homeland might be saved by it – he answered, without a single sign of pain.
After a few hours of quiet sleep the leader awoke: beside his bed sat the pale, sorrowful lady, watching his every movement, the breathing of his dreams, the opening of his eyes.
The leader summoned his aides; he asked whether the couriers had returned.
He received a satisfactory answer to every question.
The enemy had withdrawn on every side, communication had been restored among every part of his army, and the road lay open all the way to the Tisza.
– Let us move on – cried the leader, rising from his bed.
– The army has had rest enough.
– Rest enough for the army, but not for you – said his doctor, forcing him back onto his pillows, and insisting
that even if he would not sleep, he must not leave his bed for several hours, and must not think of his war plans.
The leader stared out the window at the starry night, the waning moonlight, the wooded mountains,
and as his gaze reached the horizon, he saw there the pale white mist sitting motionless in the windless night.
– What can that be?
– he asked.
– It is like some sign of a distant fire, only rather white than red.
Were it winter, I should take it for the northern lights.
What can that be?
The dreamy lady spoke at the head of his bed: "It is the white angel."
The leader looked at her questioningly.
There is a legend about it, which the common people know well.
They believe it signifies something very good.
The leader asked the lady to acquaint him with this legend,
which he would now gladly hear, since for two hours he was forbidden to think of war plans.
The lady smilingly yielded to the request, and in turn asked that he not laugh at what she was about to say, for after all it was only a legend.
Hungarians had shed one another's blood.
Some worshipped their God at springs, others before the cross; for this they fought.
The Christian king sent war against those who sacrificed white horses to the Lord of Hosts,
and after a long, bloody battle he defeated them, captured their leader, killed him, scattered their armies, and cast down their altars.
Only one band, small in number but strong in resolve, escaped into the forests of the Bükk,
where their captain's castle stood, built upon a high, steep, volcano-shaped ridge.
Time had long since erased the lord's name from memory, but his castle still stands; its maimed walls still struggle against time and storms,
and when at midnight angry tempests howl through its open windows, those dwelling in the valley believe pagan souls are shrieking there.
The lord had a beautiful daughter, whom the countryside regarded as a beneficent fairy,
who went from village to village tending the poor and healing the sick, who could not sleep if she heard someone weeping.
Yet the beautiful maiden was not Christian.
She too worshipped her fathers' god, and while the wild warriors on Örvény Rock presented their burning sacrifices to the Lord of Hosts –
where the scattered stones of a vast moss-covered altar can still be seen –
while the autumn shaman beneath the Holy Spirit Stone, in miraculously shaped niches still visible today, drew forth the snow-white stallion's red blood:
meanwhile the lord's daughter, with the fairest youths of the region, carried wreaths woven of lily and white rose to Harica Spring, as flower-offerings to the great spirit's mossy altar.
The best and fairest of the warriors was the maiden's beloved.
No one knows his name, but he must have been the best and fairest, for the best and fairest maiden was in love with him.
To this castle withdrew the surviving pagan army after Kupa's defeat, hoping to hold out here for a long while,
and at a favorable moment to sally forth again and renew the fight for their altars and their ancient gods.
The lord, however, thought deeply.
He imagined what the end of this war would be.
Boundless misery for the whole land, the never-dying flame of civil war,
hatred passing from grandson to grandson, and no prospect of victory, peace, or happiness in the homeland.
And he took pity on the people, who would thus perish in the double struggle, and one day, surrendering himself to the king with all his armies
and all his officers together, praying that he alone might fall as sacrifice, and mercy be shown his soldiers and captains.
But it happened the reverse.
He received mercy; his officers were beheaded.
Among them was his daughter's betrothed, the fairest and bravest of all the warriors.
The next day the maiden died too; on the third they buried her; on the fourth night she appeared to her father in a dream, with a pale, dead face.
Her beautiful long black hair, which was never braided and reached below her knees, had turned entirely white in the grave,
shone like silver; her hands, her face, her burial robe, everything was white as sunlit cloud.
On her brow a wreath of lily and white rose.
Thus she appeared before her sleeping father.
She said nothing, only handed him a letter, in which he read the names of all those officers whom she had delivered into his hands, and who were beheaded because of her.
The lord went mad in his dream, leaped from his bed, and as though running outward plunged headlong from the bastion onto the steep rocks below.
The castle thereafter stood empty forever; each year one stone falls from its towers, each spring one more flower grows on its deserted walls.
And when sometimes on a silent night the superstitious peasant scans the horizon and sees a distant floating whitish oval light:
the soul of the white angel is there, he whispers to himself, and takes it as a good omen, and thereafter dreams all night of fairies,
with smiling otherworldly faces, who with long silver hair, white faces, white garments like sunlit cloud, glimmer before his dreaming soul.
So ran the legend.
The commander thanked the lady for her kindness, and his restless spirit, not allowing him to rest, ordered the whole army to march at once,
and feverish, exhausted, had himself carried to his carriage; his beautiful fair head was covered with a fantastic wrapping, a blue silk kerchief, so fitting to his pale, suffering face.
When he was well on his way, he looked back, and even then saw behind him,
far on the blue horizon, the strange pale aerial phenomenon whose wondrous name is: the white angel.
It was autumn; every flower had fallen.
In a narrow, dark room the Hungarian leader lay alone.
Alone, in misery, sick, far from his homeland.
How good it would have been to die…
There he lay on his sick, fevered bed.
The painful wound on his head healed with difficulty, but a hundred times more difficult healed what he carried in his heart, and a hundred times more it pained him.
One midnight in deep sleep, as he lay on his sickbed, a white figure appeared before him.
He felt as though it were an old acquaintance, yet he could not tell whence.
Long silver hair reaching below her knees; her hands, her face, her garments, everything white as sunlit cloud.
On her brow a wreath of lily and white rose.
She bore a letter in her hand.
She laid it on the sick man's table, then remained before him long in silence,
sat there all night, and only vanished when he opened his waking eyes.
Even then it seemed to him as though he saw her flying silver hair flutter as she departed.
It was morning.
On his table lay a letter, brought to him while he slept.
The letter spoke with the voice of his homeland.
With faint hope he took it up, broke the seal, and read.
He read that thirteen of his generals had been condemned to death and executed; he alone had received mercy…
…White angel, white angel…
